title: حِكَايَةُ عَلِيِّ بْنِ بَكَّارٍ مَعَ شَمْسِ النَّهَارِ
titleEn: ʿAlī ibn Bakkār and Shams al-Nahār
part: Night 154 · ʿAlī ibn Bakkār and Shams al-Nahār, continued
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 767–772 (Night 154, continuing directly from nights-153), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm as Macnaghten prints it, except where a clear misprint has been corrected (each is noted). Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms, is preserved; clear misprints are corrected in the text, and the note on each gives the print’s reading. Obscure or doubtful forms are kept as printed, vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 154 continues the tale of ʿAlī ibn Bakkār and Shams al-Nahār. The feast in Shams al-Nahār's pavilion goes on with wine and song until a slave-girl runs in: the caliph's eunuchs are at the door. Shams al-Nahār hides her two guests, receives Masrūr and his men, and hears that Hārūn al-Rashīd is coming to her that night. She bids ʿAlī a tearful farewell and has him and Abū al-Ḥasan locked in a balcony over the garden, from which they watch the caliph arrive with his eunuchs and twenty candle-bearing slave-girls. When the singer Gharām sings of a longing like her own, Shams al-Nahār falls senseless from her chair, and in the balcony ʿAlī faints as well. A slave-girl hurries the two men out through a small iron door to the Tigris, where a boatman rows them away, and ʿAlī bids the palace farewell in two lines of verse. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ الرَّابِعَةُ وَالْخَمْسُونَ بَعْدَ الْمِائَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-rābiʿatu wa-al-khamsūna baʿda al-miʾati
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the fourth-and-fifty after the hundred,
sentences.i: And when it was the hundred and fifty-fourth night,
sentences.n: al-rābiʿa, “the fourth”, is the ordinal, feminine to agree with layla; al-khamsūn, “fifty”, keeps its cardinal form and is joined by wa-.

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُأَنَّ شَمْسَ النَّهَارِ مَلَأَتِ الْكَأْسَ وَأَعْطَتْهُ لِعَلِيِّ بْنِ بَكَّارٍ ثُمَّ أَمَرَتْ جَارِيَةً أَنْ تُغَنِّيَ فَأَنْشَدَتْ تَقُولُ هَذِهِ الْأَبْيَاتَ
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu anna Shamsa al-Nahāri malaʾati al-kaʾsa wa-aʿṭathu li-ʿAliyyi ibni Bakkārin thumma amarat jāriyatan an tughanniya fa-anshadat taqūlu hādhihi al-abyāta
sentences.l: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that Shams al-Nahār filled the cup and gave-it to ʿAlī son of Bakkār; then she-ordered a slave-girl that she-sing, and she-recited, saying these lines:
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that Shams al-Nahār filled the cup and handed it to ʿAlī ibn Bakkār. Then she ordered a slave-girl to sing, and the girl sang these lines:
sentences.n: The print runs al-saʿīd, “fortunate”, into the following anna, “that” (السعيدان); the run-together spelling is kept and pointed as one word, al-saʿīdu anna. aʿṭathu li-ʿAlī, “she gave it to ʿAlī”: aʿṭā normally takes both the person and the thing as direct objects; here the cup is the object pronoun -hu and the person comes with li-, as often in the Nights. an tughanniya, “that she should sing”: the subjunctive after an; the shadda of تغنّي is the print's own.

sentences.t:
تَشَاكَلَ دَمْعِي اِذْ جَرَى وَمُدَامَتِي * فَمِنْ مِثْلِ مَافِى الْكَأْسِ عَيْنِي تَسْكُبُ
فَوَاللّٰهِ مَا اَدْرِي اَبِالْخَمْرِ اَسْبَلَتْ * جُفُونِي اَمْ مِنْ اَدْمُعِي كُنْتُ اَشْرَبُ
sentences.tr:
tashākala damʿī idh jarā wa-mudāmatī * fa-min mithli mā fī al-kaʾsi ʿaynī taskubu
fa-wa-Allāhi mā adrī a-bi-al-khamri asbalat * jufūnī am min admuʿī kuntu ashrabu
sentences.l:
My-tear, when it-flowed, and my-wine resembled-each-other, * so from the like of what (is) in the cup my-eye pours.
And by God, I-know not: was-it with the wine (that) my-eyelids * shed, or from my-tears I-was drinking?
sentences.i:
My tears, as they flowed, grew so like my wine that my eye pours out the very likeness of what is in the cup;
by God, I cannot tell whether it was wine my eyelids shed, or whether it was my own tears I drank.
sentences.n: The pointing is the print's own, kept as printed, including the bare alif of اِذْ, اَدْرِي, اَبِالْخَمْرِ, اَسْبَلَتْ and اَدْمُعِي, where the edition marks no hamza. The metre is ṭawīl, rhyming on -abu. The print runs mā fī together and writes its yāʾ as ى (مَافِى). tashākala, “to resemble one another”, takes both of its subjects, the tears and the wine: the lover weeps tears of blood, red as the wine, until she cannot tell which she is shedding and which she is drinking. asbala, “to let fall”, is said of eyelids letting fall tears. a-bi-al-khamri, “was it wine…?”: the question particle a- stands on bi-, which here marks what the eyelids shed; am, “or”, gives the second half of the question.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا فَرَغَتْ مِنْ شِعْرِهَا شَرِبَ عَلِيُّ بْنُ بَكَّارٍ كَأْسَهُ وَرَدَّهُ إِلَى شَمْسِ النَّهَارِ فَمَلَأَتْهُ وَنَاوَلَتْهُ لِأَبِي الْحَسَنِ فَشَرِبَهُ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā faraghat min shiʿrihā shariba ʿAliyyu ibnu Bakkārin kaʾsahu wa-raddahu ilā Shamsi al-Nahāri fa-malaʾathu wa-nāwalathu li-Abī al-Ḥasani fa-sharibahu
sentences.l: And when she-finished from her-poem, ʿAlī son of Bakkār drank his-cup and returned-it to Shams al-Nahār; and she-filled-it and handed-it to Abū al-Ḥasan, and he-drank-it.
sentences.i: When she had finished her poem, ʿAlī ibn Bakkār drank off his cup and passed it back to Shams al-Nahār, who filled it and handed it to Abū al-Ḥasan, and he drank it.
sentences.n: kaʾs, “cup”, is usually feminine, but the print treats it as masculine here (raddahu, “returned it”, malaʾathu, “filled it”, sharibahu, “drank it”). nāwala, “to hand”, like aʿṭā above, takes the person with li- (li-Abī al-Ḥasan, “to Abū al-Ḥasan”). The shadda of ردّه is the print's own.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ أَخَذَتِ الْعُودَ وَقَالَتْ لَا يُغَنِّي عَلَى قَدَحِي غَيْرِي ثُمَّ شَدَّتِ الْأَوْتَارَ وَأَنْشَدَتْ تَقُولُ هَذِهِ الْأَشْعَارَ
sentences.tr: thumma akhadhati al-ʿūda wa-qālat lā yughannī ʿalā qadaḥī ghayrī thumma shaddati al-awtāra wa-anshadat taqūlu hādhihi al-ashʿāra
sentences.l: Then she-took the lute and said: There-shall-not sing over my-cup other-than-me. Then she-tightened the strings and recited, saying these verses:
sentences.i: Then she took up the lute herself and said, “No one but I shall sing over my cup.” She tightened the strings and sang these verses:
sentences.n: The singer now is Shams al-Nahār herself. ʿalā qadaḥī, “over my cup”: the song that goes with a round of drinking. shadda al-awtār, “to tighten the strings”, is to tune the lute. al-awtār and al-ashʿār rhyme, the usual small piece of sajʿ before a song.

sentences.t:
غَرَائِبُ الدَّمْعِ فِي خَدَّيْهِ تَضْطَرِبُ * وَلِلْهَوَى حُرَقٌ فِي صَدْرِهِ تَقِدُ
يَبْكِي مِنَ الْقُرْبِ خَوْفًا مِنْ تَبَاعُدِهِمْ * فَالدَّمْعُ اِنْ قَرُبُوا جَارٍ وَاِنْ بَعُدُوا
sentences.tr:
gharāʾibu al-damʿi fī khaddayhi taḍṭaribu * wa-li-al-hawā ḥuraqun fī ṣadrihi taqidu
yabkī mina al-qurbi khawfan min tabāʿudihim * fa-al-damʿu in qarubū jārin wa-in baʿudū
sentences.l:
The strange-ones of the tear on his-two-cheeks quiver, * and to the passion (are) burnings in his-breast (that) blaze;
he-weeps from the nearness for-fear of their-drawing-apart, * so the tear, if they-come-near, (is) flowing, and if they-go-far.
sentences.i:
Strange tears tremble upon his cheeks, and love has fires that blaze within his breast;
he weeps when they are near, for fear that they will go: so his tears flow if they are near, and flow if they are far.
sentences.n: The pointing is the print's own, kept as printed, including the bare alif of اِنْ and وَاِنْ. The metre is basīṭ, rhyming on -idu/-udū. gharāʾib al-damʿ, “the strange ones of the tear”, are tears that come unbidden; gharb is also the flow of tears from the eye, and the poet plays on both. li-al-hawā ḥuraqun, “passion has burnings”: li- marks the owner. The lover is spoken of as “he” and the beloved as “they”, the plural of discretion that love poetry uses for a single beloved. jārin, “flowing”, is the active participle of jarā with its final -ī dropped in the indefinite; one jārin serves both conditions, “if they are near” and “if they are far”.

sentences.t: وَقَوْلُ الْآخَرِ
sentences.tr: wa-qawlu al-ākhari
sentences.l: And the saying of the other:
sentences.i: And another poet says:
sentences.n: Short for wa-min dhālika qawlu al-ākhar, “and among them is the saying of another”: a second poem follows, though the print does not say whether Shams al-Nahār sings it too. The print writes al-ākhar with its own madda (الآخر).

sentences.t:
نَتَفَدَّاكَ سَاقِيًا قَدْ كَسَاكَ الْحُسْنُ * مِنْ فَرْقِكَ الْمُضِيءِ لِسَاقِكْ
تَشْرُقُ الشَّمْسُ مِنْ يَدَيْكَ وَمِنْ فِيكَ * الثُّرَيَّا وَالْبَدْرُ مِنْ اَطْوَاقِكْ
اِنَّ اَقْدَاحَكَ الَّتِى تَرَكَتْنِي * غَيْرَ صَاحٍ تُدَارُ مِنْ اَحْدَاقِكْ
اَوَلَيْسَ الْعَجِيبُ كَوْنُكَ بَدْرًا * كَامِلًا وَالْمُحَاقُ مِنْ عُشَّاقِكْ
آالهُ اَنْتَ اِذْ تُمِيتُ وَتُحْيِي * بِتَلَاقِيكَ مَنْ تَشَا وَفِرَاقِكْ
خَلَقَ اللّٰهُ مِنْ خَلِيقَتِكَ الْحُسْنَ * وَطِيبَ النَّسِيمِ مِنْ اَخْلَاقِكْ
مَا اَنْتَ مِنْ هَذِهِ الْبَرِيَّةِ بَلْ اَنْتَ * مَلِيكٌ اُرْسِلْتَ مِنْ خَلَّاقِكْ
sentences.tr:
natafaddāka sāqiyan qad kasāka al-ḥusnu * min farqika al-muḍīʾi li-sāqik
tashruqu al-shamsu min yadayka wa-min fīka * al-thurayyā wa-al-badru min aṭwāqik
inna aqdāḥaka allatī tarakatnī * ghayra ṣāḥin tudāru min aḥdāqik
a-wa-laysa al-ʿajību kawnuka badran * kāmilan wa-al-muḥāqu min ʿushshāqik
a-ilāhun anta idh tumītu wa-tuḥyī * bi-talāqīka man tashā wa-firāqik
khalaqa Allāhu min khalīqatika al-ḥusna * wa-ṭība al-nasīmi min akhlāqik
mā anta min hādhihi al-bariyyati bal anta * malīkun ursilta min khallāqik
sentences.l:
We-ransom-ourselves-for-you, (O) cupbearer whom the beauty has clothed * from your-parting, the shining-one, to your-shank.
The sun rises from your-two-hands, and from your-mouth * the Pleiades, and the full-moon from your-collars.
Indeed your-cups which have-left-me * other-than sober are-passed-round from your-eyes.
And is-it not the wonder, your-being a full-moon * complete, and the moon's-dark (is) among your-lovers?
A god (are) you, since you-make-die and give-life * by your-meeting whom you-will, and your-parting?
God created from your-nature the beauty, * and the sweetness of the breeze from your-character.
You (are) not of this creation; rather you (are) * a king you-were-sent from your-Creator.
sentences.i:
We would give our lives for you, O cupbearer, clothed in beauty from the shining parting of your hair down to your feet.
The sun rises from your hands, from your mouth the Pleiades, and the full moon from the collar of your robe.
The cups that have left me far from sober are passed round from your eyes.
Is it not a wonder that you should be the full moon, whole and complete, while the dark of the moon is found among your lovers?
Are you a god, that you give death and life, to whom you will, by your coming and your going?
God made beauty out of your nature, and the sweetness of the breeze out of your ways.
You are not of this world's creatures: you are a king sent down from your Creator.
sentences.n: The print has بديك, a misprint for يديك, corrected here. Otherwise the pointing is the print's own, kept as printed, including the bare alif of اَطْوَاقِكْ, اِنَّ, اَنْتَ and اُرْسِلْتَ, where the edition marks no hamza. The metre is khafīf, every line rhyming on -āqik with a pausal sukūn (لِسَاقِكْ). The beloved is a youth, the cupbearer (sāqī), and the first line already puns on sāqī and sāq, “shank”. natafaddāka, “we ransom ourselves for you”, the lover's oath of devotion. In line 2 the sun in his hands is the wine he pours, the Pleiades in his mouth are his teeth, and the full moon rising from his collar is his face. In line 3 his eyes are the cups that make the poet drunk. Line 4: laysa here governs the whole clause, “is it not (the case that) the wonder is your being a full moon”, so al-ʿajību and kawnuka are both nominative. al-muḥāq is the dark of the month, when the moon cannot be seen: his lovers waste away to nothing while he stays full. In line 5 the print sets آالهُ, alif with madda followed by a second alif: the interrogative a- before ilāhun, “a god”, which Classical spelling writes أَإِلٰهٌ. The madda probably records the reading āʾilāhun, with a long ā between the two hamzas, as some Qurʾān readers pronounce the same phrase (Q 27:60); the letters are kept, and the print gives a single ḍamma where the metre wants the tanwīn of ilāhun. tashā stands for tashāʾu, “you will”, its hamza dropped for the metre. Line 6 plays on khalaqa, “created”, khalīqa, “nature”, and akhlāq, “character”. Line 7 recalls the women's cry over Joseph in the Qurʾān (12:31), “this is no mortal”; malīk is “king”, and khallāq, “the Creator”, the intensive form of khāliq.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَ عَلِيُّ بْنُ بَكَّارٍ وَأَبُو الْحَسَنِ وَالْحَاضِرُونَ شِعْرَ شَمْسِ النَّهَارِ كَادُوا أَنْ يَطِيرُوا مِنَ الطَّرَبِ وَلَعِبُوا وَضَحِكُوا
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿa ʿAliyyu ibnu Bakkārin wa-Abū al-Ḥasani wa-al-ḥāḍirūna shiʿra Shamsi al-Nahāri kādū an yaṭīrū mina al-ṭarabi wa-laʿibū wa-ḍaḥikū
sentences.l: And when ʿAlī son of Bakkār and Abū al-Ḥasan and the present-ones heard the verse of Shams al-Nahār, they-were-near-to fly from the delight, and they-played and laughed.
sentences.i: When ʿAlī ibn Bakkār, Abū al-Ḥasan and all who were there heard Shams al-Nahār's verses, they nearly flew for joy, and they made merry and laughed.
sentences.n: kāda, “be on the point of”, here takes an before its verb, which Classical usage with kāda usually leaves out. ṭarab, the rapture that music and poetry stir.

sentences.t: فَبَيْنَمَاهُمْ عَلَى هَذَا الْحَالِ وَإِذَا بِجَارِيَةٍ أَقْبَلَتْ وَهِيَ تَرْتَعِدُ مِنَ الْخَوْفِ وَقَالَتْ يَاسَيِّدَتِي خُدَّامُ أَمِيرِالْمُؤْمِنِينَ بِالْبَابِ وَهُمْ عَفِيفٌ وَمَسْرُورٌ وَمَرْجَانُ وَغَيْرُهُمْ مِنَ الْخُدَّامِ لَمْ أَعْرِفْهُمْ
sentences.tr: fa-baynamāhum ʿalā hādhā al-ḥāli wa-idhā bi-jāriyatin aqbalat wa-hiya tartaʿidu mina al-khawfi wa-qālat yā sayyidatī khuddāmu amīri al-muʾminīna bi-al-bābi wa-hum ʿAfīfun wa-Masrūrun wa-Marjānu wa-ghayruhum mina al-khuddāmi lam aʿrifhum
sentences.l: And while-they (were) upon this state, behold, a slave-girl came-forward, and she trembling from the fear, and she-said: O my-lady, the servants of the Commander of the Believers (are) at the door, and they (are) ʿAfīf and Masrūr and Marjān, and others-of-them of the servants I-did-not know-them.
sentences.i: While they were so engaged, a slave-girl suddenly came in, trembling with fear, and said, “My lady, the eunuchs of the Commander of the Faithful are at the door: ʿAfīf, Masrūr, Marjān and others I do not know.”
sentences.n: wa-idhā bi-, “and behold”: the bi- only marks what appears. khuddām, “servants”, here the palace eunuchs; Masrūr is the caliph's eunuch and swordbearer, familiar from many tales. ḥāl, “state”, is usually feminine, but the masculine hādhā goes with it here. lam aʿrifhum, “I did not know them”, is a relative clause on an indefinite (“others”), so it needs no alladhīna and takes a resumptive -hum. The print runs yā sayyidatī and amīr al-muʾminīn together as single words.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعُوا كَلَامَ الْجَارِيَةِ كَادُوا أَنْ يَهْلِكُوا مِنَ الْخَوْفِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿū kalāma al-jāriyati kādū an yahlikū mina al-khawfi
sentences.l: And when they-heard the speech of the slave-girl, they-were-near-to perish from the fear.
sentences.i: When they heard what the slave-girl said, they all but died of fright.
sentences.n: “They” are the two men and the company with them; the text does not say more precisely.

sentences.t: فَضَحِكَتْ شَمْسُ النَّهَارِ وَقَالَتْ لَاتَخَافُوا
sentences.tr: fa-ḍaḥikat Shamsu al-Nahāri wa-qālat lā takhāfū
sentences.l: And Shams al-Nahār laughed and said: Do-not fear.
sentences.i: But Shams al-Nahār laughed and said, “Don't be afraid.”
sentences.n: lā with the jussive (takhāfū) forbids: “do not fear”. The print runs لا تخافوا together as one word.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ قَالَتْ لِلْجَارِيَةِ رُدِّي عَلَيْهِمُ الْجَوَابَ بِقَدْرِ مَانَتَحَوَّلُ مِنْ هَذَا الْمَكَانِ
sentences.tr: thumma qālat li-al-jāriyati ruddī ʿalayhimu al-jawāba bi-qadri mā nataḥawwalu min hādhā al-makāni
sentences.l: Then she-said to the slave-girl: Return upon-them the answer by-the-measure-of what we-move from this place.
sentences.i: Then she said to the slave-girl, “Give them an answer, and take as long over it as we need to get away from this place.”
sentences.n: radda ʿalayhi al-jawāba, “return the answer upon him”, is simply “answer him”. bi-qadri mā, “by the measure of what”, means “for as long as”. The print runs ما نتحول together; the shadda in ردّي is the print's own.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّهَا أَمَرَتْ بِغَلْقِ بَابِ الْقُبَّةِ وَأَرْخَتْ عَلَى أَبْوَابِهَا السَّتَائِرَ وَهُمْ فِيهَا وَأَغْلَقَتْ بَابَ الْقَاعَةِ
sentences.tr: thumma innahā amarat bi-ghalqi bābi al-qubbati wa-arkhat ʿalā abwābihā al-satāʾira wa-hum fīhā wa-aghlaqat bāba al-qāʿati
sentences.l: Then indeed-she ordered the shutting of the door of the dome, and let-down over its-doors the curtains, and they (were) in-it, and she-locked the door of the hall.
sentences.i: Then she had the door of the domed chamber shut, with the two men inside, let the curtains fall over its doors, and locked the door of the hall.
sentences.n: amara bi-, “order (something)”: the thing ordered takes bi-. qubba, “dome”, and so a domed chamber or pavilion; qāʿa, the great hall of a house. wa-hum fīhā, “and they in it”, is a circumstantial clause: the two men are shut inside. ghalq, “shutting”, is a rarer verbal noun beside ighlāq.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ خَرَجَتْ مِنْ بَابِ السِّرِّ إِلَى الْبُسْتَانِ وَجَلَسَتْ عَلَى سَرِيرٍ لَهَا هُنَاكَ
sentences.tr: thumma kharajat min bābi al-sirri ilā al-bustāni wa-jalasat ʿalā sarīrin lahā hunāka
sentences.l: Then she-went-out by the door of the secret to the garden, and sat on a couch of-hers there.
sentences.i: Then she went out by the private door into the garden and sat down on a couch of hers that stood there.
sentences.n: bāb al-sirr, “the door of the secret”, a private or hidden door. The shadda in السرّ is the print's own.

sentences.t: وَأَمَرَتْ جَارِيَةً أَنْ تَكْبِسَ رِجْلَيْهَا وَأَمَرَتْ بَقِيَّةَ الْجَوَارِي أَنْ يَمْضِينَ إِلَى أَمَاكِنِهِنَّ وَأَمَرَتِ الْجَارِيَةَ أَنْ تَدْعُوَ مَنْ بِالْبَابِ لِيَدْخُلَ
sentences.tr: wa-amarat jāriyatan an takbisa rijlayhā wa-amarat baqiyyata al-jawārī an yamḍīna ilā amākinihinna wa-amarati al-jāriyata an tadʿuwa man bi-al-bābi li-yadkhula
sentences.l: And she-ordered a slave-girl that she-press her-two-feet, and ordered the rest of the slave-girls that they(f.) go to their(f.)-places, and ordered the slave-girl that she-call who (was) at the door, to-enter.
sentences.i: She told one slave-girl to rub her feet, sent the rest of the slave-girls off to their quarters, and told the maid to call in whoever was at the door.
sentences.n: kabasa, “press”, of the limbs, to knead or massage them, a common service of a slave-girl; rijl is both leg and foot. amara, “order”, here takes the person ordered as its object and the deed with an and the subjunctive. li-yadkhula, “so that he enter”: li- with the subjunctive gives the purpose. The fatḥa on مَن is the print's own.

sentences.t: فَدَخَلَ مَسْرُورٌ وَمَنْ مَعَهُ وَكَانُوا عِشْرِينَ وَبِأَيْدِيهِمُ السُّيُوفُ فَسَلَّمُوا عَلَى شَمْسِ النَّهَارِ
sentences.tr: fa-dakhala Masrūrun wa-man maʿahu wa-kānū ʿishrīna wa-bi-aydīhimu al-suyūfu fa-sallamū ʿalā Shamsi al-Nahāri
sentences.l: And Masrūr entered and who (was) with-him, and they-were twenty, and in their-hands the swords; and they-gave-greeting upon Shams al-Nahār.
sentences.i: In came Masrūr and those with him, twenty of them, with drawn swords in their hands, and they greeted Shams al-Nahār.
sentences.n: wa-bi-aydīhimu al-suyūfu, “and in their hands the swords”, is a circumstantial clause. sallama ʿalā, “greet”: the greeting of peace is wished “upon” the one greeted.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ لَهُمْ لِمَ جِئْتُمْ
sentences.tr: fa-qālat lahum lima jiʾtum
sentences.l: And she-said to-them: Why have-you-come?
sentences.i: “Why have you come?” she asked them.

sentences.t: فَقَالُوا إِنَّ أَمِيرَ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ يُسَلِّمُ عَلَيْكِ وَقَدِ اسْتَوْحَشَ لِرُؤْيَتِكِ وَيُخْبِرُكِ أَنَّهُ كَانَ عِنْدَهُ الْيَوْمَ سُرُورٌ وَحَظٌّ زَائِدٌ وَأَحَبَّ أَنْ يَكُونَ خِتَامُ السُّرُورِ بِوُجُودِكِ فِي هَذِهِ السَّاعَةِ فَهَلْ تَأْتِينَ عِنْدَهُ أَوْ يَأْتِي عِنْدَكِ
sentences.tr: fa-qālū inna amīra al-muʾminīna yusallimu ʿalayki wa-qadi istawḥasha li-ruʾyatiki wa-yukhbiruki annahu kāna ʿindahu al-yawma surūrun wa-ḥaẓẓun zāʾidun wa-aḥabba an yakūna khitāmu al-surūri bi-wujūdiki fī hādhihi al-sāʿati fa-hal taʾtīna ʿindahu aw yaʾtī ʿindaki
sentences.l: And they-said: Indeed the Commander of the Believers greets you, and he-has-grown-lonely for your-sight, and he-tells-you that there-was with-him today gladness and exceeding pleasure, and he-wished that the seal of the gladness be with your-presence in this hour; so will you-come to-him, or shall-he-come to-you?
sentences.i: They said, “The Commander of the Faithful sends you his greeting. He has been missing the sight of you, and he tells you that he has had great joy and pleasure today, and he wishes to crown his joy with your company at this hour. Will you come to him, or shall he come to you?”
sentences.n: istawḥasha li-, “feel lonely for”, is to miss someone. ḥaẓẓ, properly “lot, good fortune”, is here the colloquial “pleasure, a good time”. khitām, “seal, close”: the ending that crowns the day. atā ʿinda, “come at (someone's)”, for Classical atā ilā, “come to”, is colloquial; the hamza on تأتين and يأتي is the print's own. The messengers address her with the feminine -ki throughout.

sentences.t: فَقَامَتْ وَقَبَّلَتِ الْأَرْضَ وَقَالَتْ سَمْعًا وَطَاعَةً لِأَمْرِ أَمِيرِ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ
sentences.tr: fa-qāmat wa-qabbalati al-arḍa wa-qālat samʿan wa-ṭāʿatan li-amri amīri al-muʾminīna
sentences.l: And she-rose and kissed the ground and said: Hearing and obedience to the command of the Commander of the Believers.
sentences.i: She rose, kissed the ground, and answered with hearing and obedience to the command of the Commander of the Faithful.
sentences.n: She kisses the ground before the caliph's messengers as homage to the caliph himself. samʿan wa-ṭāʿatan, “hearing and obedience”, is the stock reply to a command; the accusatives depend on an unspoken verb, “(I give)”.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ أَمَرَتْ بِإِحْضَارِ الْقَهْرَمَانَاتِ وَالْجَوَارِي فَحَضَرْنَ وَأَظْهَرَتْ لَهُنَّ أَنَّهَا مُقْبِلَةٌ عَلَى مَا أَمَرَ بِهِ الْخَلِيفَةُ وَكَانَ الْمَكَانُ كَامِلًا فِي جَمِيعِ أُمُورِهِ
sentences.tr: thumma amarat bi-iḥḍāri al-qahramānāti wa-al-jawārī fa-ḥaḍarna wa-aẓharat lahunna annahā muqbilatun ʿalā mā amara bihi al-khalīfatu wa-kāna al-makānu kāmilan fī jamīʿi umūrihi
sentences.l: Then she-ordered the bringing of the stewardesses and the slave-girls, and they(f.)-came; and she-showed to-them that she (was) turning-toward what the caliph ordered of-it; and the place was complete in all its-matters.
sentences.i: Then she had the stewardesses and slave-girls summoned, and when they came she let them see that she was setting about what the caliph had bidden; and the place was already perfectly appointed in every respect.
sentences.n: qahramāna (from Persian), a stewardess or housekeeper set over a great lady's household. aqbala ʿalā, “turn toward”, to set about a task. amara bi-, “order (something)”: mā amara bihi, “what he ordered”; the hamza on أمر is the print's own.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ قَالَتْ لِلْخُدَّامِ امْضُوا إِلَى أَمِيرِ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ وَأَخْبِرُوهُ أَنَّنِي فِى انْتِظَارِهِ بَعْدَ قَلِيلٍ إِلَى أَنْ أُهَيِّءَ لَهُ مَكَانًا بِالْفُرُشِ وَالْأَمْتِعَةِ
sentences.tr: thumma qālat li-al-khuddāmi imḍū ilā amīri al-muʾminīna wa-akhbirūhu annanī fī intiẓārihi baʿda qalīlin ilā an uhayyiʾa lahu makānan bi-al-furushi wa-al-amtiʿati
sentences.l: Then she-said to the servants: Go to the Commander of the Believers and tell-him that-I (am) in awaiting-him after a little, until I-prepare for-him a place with the carpets and the furnishings.
sentences.i: Then she said to the eunuchs, “Go to the Commander of the Faithful and tell him that I shall be awaiting him shortly, as soon as I have made a place ready for him with carpets and furnishings.”
sentences.n: The print writes the final hamza of uhayyiʾa on the line (اهيّء), where Classical spelling seats it on a yāʾ (أهيّئ); the shadda is the print's own. furush, plural of firāsh, carpets and cushions spread for sitting; amtiʿa, plural of matāʿ, household goods.

sentences.t: فَمَضَى الْخُدَّامُ مُسْرِعِينَ إِلَى أَمِيرِ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ
sentences.tr: fa-maḍā al-khuddāmu musriʿīna ilā amīri al-muʾminīna
sentences.l: And the servants went hastening to the Commander of the Believers.
sentences.i: The eunuchs hurried off to the Commander of the Faithful.
sentences.n: musriʿīna, “hastening”, is a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl).

sentences.t: وَأَمَّا شَمْسُ النَّهَارِ فَإِنَّهَا خَلَعَتْ ثِيَابَهَا وَدَخَلَتْ إِلَى مَعْشُوقِهَا عَلِيِّ بْنِ بَكَّارٍ وَضَمَّتْهُ إِلَى صَدْرِهَا وَوَدَّعَتْهُ فَبَكَى بُكَاءً شَدِيدًا
sentences.tr: wa-ammā Shamsu al-Nahāri fa-innahā khalaʿat thiyābahā wa-dakhalat ilā maʿshūqihā ʿAliyyi ibni Bakkārin wa-ḍammathu ilā ṣadrihā wa-waddaʿathu fa-bakā bukāʾan shadīdan
sentences.l: And as-for Shams al-Nahār, indeed-she took-off her-clothes and went-in to her-beloved ʿAlī son of Bakkār, and pressed-him to her-breast and bade-him-farewell; and he-wept a-severe weeping.
sentences.i: As for Shams al-Nahār, she took off her clothes and went in to her beloved, ʿAlī ibn Bakkār, pressed him to her breast and bade him farewell; and he wept bitterly.
sentences.n: wa-ammā … fa-innahā, “as for … she”, turns the story to another character; ammā is answered by fa-. bakā bukāʾan shadīdan, “wept a severe weeping”: the cognate accusative strengthens the verb. The shaddas in ضمّته and ودّعته are the print's own.

sentences.t: وَقَالَ يَاسَيِّدَتِي إِنَّ هَذَا الْوَدَاعَ سَبَبًا لِتَلَفِ نَفْسِي وَهَلَاكِ رُوحِي وَلَكِنْ أَسْأَلُ اللَّهَ أَنْ يَرْزُقَنِي الصَّبْرَ عَلَي مَا بَلَانِي بِهِ مِنْ مَحَبَّتِي
sentences.tr: wa-qāla yā sayyidatī inna hādhā al-wadāʿa sababan li-talafi nafsī wa-halāki rūḥī wa-lākin asʾalu Allāha an yarzuqanī al-ṣabra ʿalā mā balānī bihi min maḥabbatī
sentences.l: And he-said: O my-lady, indeed this farewell (is) a-cause for the ruin of my-soul and the perishing of my-spirit; but I-ask God that He-grant-me the patience upon what He-afflicted-me with-it of my-love.
sentences.i: He said, “My lady, this farewell will be the ruin of my soul and the death of my spirit; but I ask God to grant me patience to bear the love with which He has afflicted me.”
sentences.n: inna hādhā al-wadāʿa sababan: Classical grammar puts the predicate of inna in the nominative (sababun); the print's accusative sababan, with its alif, is a Middle Arabic feature and is kept. The print spells ʿalā, “upon”, with a dotted yāʾ (علي); it is read ʿalā. balā bi-, “afflict with”: bi- takes the affliction, which min maḥabbatī, “(consisting) of my love”, then names. The print runs yā sayyidatī together; the shadda in ياسيّدتي and the hamza on اسأل are the print's own.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ لَهُ شَمْسُ النَّهَارِ وَاللَّهِ مَايَصِيرُ فِى التَّلَفِ إِلَّا أَنَا فَإِنَّكَ قَدْ تَخْرُجُ إِلَى السُّوقِ وَتَجْتَمِعُ بِمَنْ يُسَلِّيكَ فَتَكُونُ مَصُونًا وَغَرَامُكَ مَكْنُونًا
sentences.tr: fa-qālat lahu Shamsu al-Nahāri wa-Allāhi mā yaṣīru fī al-talafi illā anā fa-innaka qad takhruju ilā al-sūqi wa-tajtamiʿu bi-man yusallīka fa-takūnu maṣūnan wa-gharāmuka maknūnan
sentences.l: And Shams al-Nahār said to-him: By God, none comes-to-be in the ruin except I; for you may go-out to the market and meet with whoever diverts-you, and so you-will-be guarded, and your-passion hidden.
sentences.i: Shams al-Nahār said to him, “By God, I am the only one who will come to ruin. You can go out to the market and be with people who will take your mind off it, and so stay safe, with your passion kept hidden.
sentences.n: mā yaṣīru … illā anā, “there does not come to be … except I”: she alone will suffer. The print runs ما يصير together. ijtamaʿa bi-, “meet with, keep company with”. maṣūnan … maknūnan is a rhymed pair (sajʿ); maknūnan is accusative as though takūnu still governed it: “and (with) your passion hidden”. Her speech runs on through the next three units.

sentences.t: وَأَمَّا أَنَا فَإِنِّي أَقَعُ فِى الْعَنَاءِ وَالتَّعَبِ وَلَا أَجِدُ مَنْ يُسَلِّينِي
sentences.tr: wa-ammā anā fa-innī aqaʿu fī al-ʿanāʾi wa-al-taʿabi wa-lā ajidu man yusallīnī
sentences.l: And as-for I, indeed-I fall into the distress and the weariness, and I-do-not find who diverts-me,
sentences.i: But as for me, I shall fall into misery and weariness, and find no one to comfort me,
sentences.n: al-ʿanāʾ wa-al-taʿab, “distress and weariness”, a near-synonym pair for emphasis.

sentences.t: خُصُوصًا وَقَدْ وَعَدْتُ الْخَلِيفَةَ بِمِيعَادٍ فَرُبَّمَا يَلْحَقُنِي مِنْ ذَلِكَ عَظِيمُ الْخَطَرِ بِسَبَبِ شَوْقِي إِلَيْكَ وَحُبِّي لَكَ وَتَعَشُّقِي فِيكَ وَتَأَسُّفِى عَلَى مُفَارَقَتِكَ
sentences.tr: khuṣūṣan wa-qad waʿadtu al-khalīfata bi-mīʿādin fa-rubbamā yalḥaqunī min dhālika ʿaẓīmu al-khaṭari bi-sababi shawqī ilayka wa-ḥubbī laka wa-taʿashshuqī fīka wa-taʾassufī ʿalā mufāraqatika
sentences.l: especially and I-have promised the caliph a-meeting; so perhaps there-will-overtake-me from that the-great of the danger, by reason of my-longing for-you and my-love for-you and my-being-enamoured of-you and my-grieving over your-parting.
sentences.i: especially now that I have promised the caliph a meeting. Great danger may well come upon me from it, because of my longing for you, my love for you, my passion for you and my grief at parting from you.
sentences.n: khuṣūṣan wa-qad, “especially, (it being) that”, ties on the circumstance that makes things worse. waʿada bi-, “promise (something)”: bi- takes the thing promised. ʿaẓīm al-khaṭar, “the great of the danger”, sets the adjective before its noun in iḍāfa for emphasis: “great danger”. taʿashshaqa fī, “be enamoured of”, takes fī. The print writes taʾassufī with a final ى and with its own hamza; the shadda in تعشّقي is the print's.

sentences.t: فَبِأَيِّ لِسَانٍ أُغَنِّي وَبِأَيِّ قَلْبٍ أَحْضُرُ عِنْدَ الْخَلِيفَةِ وَبِأَيِّ كَلَامٍ أُنَادِمُ أَمِيرَ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ وَبِأَيِّ نَظَرٍ أَنْظُرُ إِلَى مَكَانٍ مَا أَنْتَ فِيهِ وَكَيْفَ أَكُونُ فِي حَضْرَةٍ لَمْ تَكُنْ بِهَا وَبِأَيِّ ذَوْقٍ أَشْرَبُ مُدَامًا مَا أَنْتَ حَاضِرُهُ
sentences.tr: fa-bi-ayyi lisānin ughannī wa-bi-ayyi qalbin aḥḍuru ʿinda al-khalīfati wa-bi-ayyi kalāmin unādimu amīra al-muʾminīna wa-bi-ayyi naẓarin anẓuru ilā makānin mā anta fīhi wa-kayfa akūnu fī ḥaḍratin lam takun bihā wa-bi-ayyi dhawqin ashrabu mudāman mā anta ḥāḍiruhu
sentences.l: So with which tongue shall-I-sing, and with which heart shall-I-attend before the caliph, and with which speech shall-I-keep-company-with the Commander of the Believers, and with which look shall-I-look at a place you (are) not in-it, and how shall-I-be in a gathering you-were-not in-it, and with which relish shall-I-drink wine you (are) not present-at-it?
sentences.i: With what tongue can I sing, with what heart can I wait upon the caliph, with what words can I keep the Commander of the Faithful company? How can I look upon a place where you are not, how can I sit in a gathering without you, and with what relish can I drink wine that you are not there to share?”
sentences.n: The repeated bi-ayyi …, “with which …?”, builds a rhetorical crescendo; bi- is “with”, the means. In mā anta fīhi and mā anta ḥāḍiruhu, mā is the negative, “you are not”, in relative clauses on indefinite nouns. nādama, “be boon companion to”, to drink and talk with someone; ḥaḍra, “presence”, a gathering held in someone's presence. The hamzas and shaddas in بأيّ and the shadda in اغنّي are the print's own.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهَا أَبُو الْحَسَنِ لَا تَتَحَيَّرِي وَاصْبِرِي وَلَا تَغْفُلِي عَنْ مُنَادَمَةِ أَمِيرِ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ هَذِهِ اللَّيْلَةَ وَلَاتُظْهِرِي لَهُ التَّهَاوُنَ وَتَجَلَّدِي
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahā Abū al-Ḥasani lā tataḥayyarī wa-iṣbirī wa-lā taghfulī ʿan munādamati amīri al-muʾminīna hādhihi al-laylata wa-lā tuẓhirī lahu al-tahāwuna wa-tajalladī
sentences.l: And Abū al-Ḥasan said to-her: Do-not be-bewildered, and be-patient, and do-not be-heedless of the boon-companionship of the Commander of the Believers this night, and do-not show to-him the slackness, and be-firm.
sentences.i: Abū al-Ḥasan said to her, “Do not lose your head. Be patient, and do not fail to keep the Commander of the Faithful good company tonight; show him no indifference, and steel yourself.”
sentences.n: lā with the jussive forbids: lā tataḥayyarī, “do not be at a loss”. tahāwun, “making light of a thing”, slackness. tajallada, “make oneself tough (jild, skin)”, to bear up. The print runs لا تظهري together; the shadda in تجلّدي is the print's own.

sentences.t: فَبَيْنَمَاهُمْ كَذَلِكَ وَإِذَا بِجَارِيَةٍ جَاءَتْ وَقَالَتْ يَاسَيِّدَتِي جَاءَ غِلْمَانُ أَمِيرِ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ
sentences.tr: fa-baynamāhum ka-dhālika wa-idhā bi-jāriyatin jāʾat wa-qālat yā sayyidatī jāʾa ghilmānu amīri al-muʾminīna
sentences.l: And while-they (were) thus, behold, a slave-girl came and said: O my-lady, the pages of the Commander of the Believers have-come.
sentences.i: While they were talking so, a slave-girl came in and said, “My lady, the pages of the Commander of the Faithful are here.”
sentences.n: ghilmān, plural of ghulām, “lad”, young household servants or pages.

sentences.t: فَنَهَضَتْ قَائِمَةً وَقَالَتْ لِلْجَارِيَةِ خُذِي أَبَا الْحَسَنِ وَرَفِيقَهُ وَاقْصِدِي بِهِمَا أَعْلَى الرَّوْشَنِ الْمُطِلِّ عَلَى الْبُسْتَانِ وَدَعِيهِمَا هُنَاكَ إِلَى أَنْ يَدْخُلَ الظَّلَامُ فَتَحَيَّلِي فِي خُرُوجِهِمَا
sentences.tr: fa-nahaḍat qāʾimatan wa-qālat li-al-jāriyati khudhī Abā al-Ḥasani wa-rafīqahu wa-iqṣidī bihimā aʿlā al-rawshani al-muṭilli ʿalā al-bustāni wa-daʿīhimā hunāka ilā an yadkhula al-ẓalāmu fa-taḥayyalī fī khurūjihimā
sentences.l: And she-rose standing and said to the slave-girl: Take Abū al-Ḥasan and his-companion and make with-the-two for the top of the balcony overlooking the garden, and leave-the-two there until the darkness enters; then contrive in their-going-out.
sentences.i: She sprang to her feet and said to the slave-girl, “Take Abū al-Ḥasan and his companion up to the balcony overlooking the garden and leave them there until dark; then find some way to get them out.”
sentences.n: nahaḍat qāʾimatan, “she rose standing”, a common pleonasm. qaṣada bi-, “make for (a place) with”, is to take someone there. A rawshan (from Persian) is a projecting window or balcony, usually latticed, here an upper room looking over the garden. taḥayyala fī, “use a stratagem in”: contrive.

sentences.t: فَأَخَذَتْهُمَا الْجَارِيَةُ وَأَطْلَعَتْهُمَا فِى الرَّوْشَنِ وَأَغْلَقَتِ الْبَابَ عَلَيْهِمَا وَمَضَتْ إِلَى حَالِ سَبِيلِهَا
sentences.tr: fa-akhadhathumā al-jāriyatu wa-aṭlaʿathumā fī al-rawshani wa-aghlaqati al-bāba ʿalayhimā wa-maḍat ilā ḥāli sabīlihā
sentences.l: And the slave-girl took-the-two and brought-the-two-up into the balcony, and shut the door upon-the-two, and went to the state of her-way.
sentences.i: The slave-girl took them, brought them up into the balcony, locked the door on them and went about her business.
sentences.n: aṭlaʿa, “make go up”, here with fī, “up into”. maḍā ilā ḥāli sabīlihi, “go to the state of one's way”, is to go about one's own affairs.

sentences.t: فَجَلَسَا يَنْظُرَانِ عَلَى الْبُسْتَانِ
sentences.tr: fa-jalasā yanẓurāni ʿalā al-bustāni
sentences.l: And the-two sat looking upon the garden.
sentences.i: And the two of them sat looking out over the garden.
sentences.n: jalasā and yanẓurāni are dual, for the two men. naẓara ʿalā, “look upon”, beside Classical naẓara ilā: here looking down over the garden.

sentences.t: وَإِذَا بِالْخَلِيفَةِ قَدِمَ وَبَيْنَ يَدَيْهِ نَحْوُ مِائَةِ خَادِمٍ بِأَيْدِيهِمُ السُّيُوفُ وَحَوَالَيْهِ عِشْرُونَ جَارِيَةً كَأَنَّهُنَّ الْأَقْمَارُ وَعَلَيْهِنَّ أَفْخَرُ مَا يَكُونُ مِنَ الْمَلْبُوسِ
sentences.tr: wa-idhā bi-al-khalīfati qadima wa-bayna yadayhi naḥwu miʾati khādimin bi-aydīhimu al-suyūfu wa-ḥawālayhi ʿishrūna jāriyatan ka-annahunna al-aqmāru wa-ʿalayhinna afkharu mā yakūnu mina al-malbūsi
sentences.l: And behold, the caliph arrived, and between his-hands about a hundred eunuchs, in their-hands the swords; and around-him twenty slave-girls, as-if they (were) the moons, and upon-them(f.) the most-splendid of what can-be of the clothing.
sentences.i: And then the caliph arrived, with about a hundred eunuchs going before him, swords in their hands, and around him twenty slave-girls like so many moons, dressed in the most splendid clothes there could be.
sentences.n: wa-idhā bi-al-khalīfa qadima, “and behold, the caliph arrived”: after idhā of surprise the bi- only marks who appears. khādim, “servant”, in a palace usually a eunuch. bayna yadayhi, “between his hands”, means before him. bi-aydīhim, “in their hands”: the bi- here means “in”. afkhar mā yakūn, “the most splendid of what can be”, the finest possible.

sentences.t: وَعَلَى رَأْسِ كُلِّ وَاحِدَةٍ تَاجٌ مُكَلَّلٌ بِالْجَوَاهِرِ وَالْيَوَاقِيتِ وَفِي يَدِ كُلِّ وَاحِدَةٍ شَمْعَةٌ مَوْقُودَةٌ
sentences.tr: wa-ʿalā raʾsi kulli wāḥidatin tājun mukallalun bi-al-jawāhiri wa-al-yawāqīti wa-fī yadi kulli wāḥidatin shamʿatun mawqūdatun
sentences.l: And on the head of every one (was) a crown wreathed with the jewels and the rubies, and in the hand of every one a candle, lit.
sentences.i: Each wore on her head a crown set with jewels and rubies, and each held a lighted candle in her hand.
sentences.n: mukallal bi-, “wreathed, set with”: the bi- names what the crown is set with. yawāqīt, plural of yāqūt, “ruby” (also sapphire). mawqūd, “kindled, lit”, the passive participle of waqada.

sentences.t: وَالْخَلِيفَةُ يَمْشِي بَيْنَهُنَّ وَهُنَّ مُحِيطَاتٌ بِهِ مِنْ كُلِّ نَاحِيَةٍ وَقُدَّامَهُ مَسْرُورٌ وَعَفِيفٌ وَوَصِيفٌ وَهُوَ يَتَمَايَلُ بَيْنَهُمْ
sentences.tr: wa-al-khalīfatu yamshī baynahunna wa-hunna muḥīṭātun bihi min kulli nāḥiyatin wa-quddāmahu Masrūrun wa-ʿAfīfun wa-Waṣīfun wa-huwa yatamāyalu baynahum
sentences.l: And the caliph walking among-them(f.), and they(f.) surrounding him from every side; and before-him Masrūr and ʿAfīf and Waṣīf; and he swaying among-them.
sentences.i: The caliph walked among them, and they surrounded him on every side, with Masrūr, ʿAfīf and Waṣīf going ahead of him; and he swayed as he went among them.
sentences.n: aḥāṭa bi-, “surround”: the verb takes what is surrounded with bi-, so muḥīṭāt bihi, “surrounding him”. Masrūr, ʿAfīf and Waṣīf are the caliph's eunuchs. yatamāyalu, “sways to and fro”: the gait of a great man at ease, or of one who has drunk; the text does not say which.

sentences.t: فَقَامَتْ لَهُ شَمْسُ النَّهَارِ وَجَمِيعُ مَنْ عِنْدَهَا مِنَ الْجَوَارِي فَلَاقَيْنَهُ مِنْ بَابِ الْبُسْتَانِ وَقَبَّلْنَ الْأَرْضَ بَيْنَ يَدَيْهِ وَلَمْ يَزَلْنَ سَائِرَاتٍ أَمَامَهُ إِلَى أَنْ جَلَسَ عَلَى السَّرِيرِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāmat lahu Shamsu al-Nahāri wa-jamīʿu man ʿindahā mina al-jawārī fa-lāqaynahu min bābi al-bustāni wa-qabbalna al-arḍa bayna yadayhi wa-lam yazalna sāʾirātin amāmahu ilā an jalasa ʿalā al-sarīri
sentences.l: And Shams al-Nahār rose for-him, and all who (were) with-her of the slave-girls, and they(f.)-met-him at the gate of the garden, and they(f.)-kissed the ground between his-hands, and they(f.)-ceased-not going before-him until he sat on the couch.
sentences.i: Shams al-Nahār rose to receive him, and so did all the slave-girls about her; they met him at the garden gate and kissed the ground before him, and went on walking ahead of him until he had taken his seat on the throne.
sentences.n: qāma lahu, “rose for him”: to stand in someone's honour; li- (la- before a pronoun) marks the one honoured. lāqaynahu, “they (f.) met him”, is feminine plural: Shams al-Nahār is counted in with her slave-girls. lam yazalna, “they did not cease”, with a participle, “they kept on”. sarīr, a couch or raised seat, here the caliph's throne. The shadda in قبّلن is the print's own.

sentences.t: وَالَّذِينَ فِى الْبُسْتَانِ مِنَ الْجَوَارِي وَالْخَدَمِ وَقَعُوا جَمِيعًا بَيْنَ يَدَيْهِ
sentences.tr: wa-alladhīna fī al-bustāni mina al-jawārī wa-al-khadami waqaʿū jamīʿan bayna yadayhi
sentences.l: And those who (were) in the garden, of the slave-girls and the servants, fell all-together between his-hands.
sentences.i: And all who were in the garden, slave-girls and servants alike, threw themselves down before him.
sentences.n: waqaʿa bayna yadayhi, “fell between his hands”, to prostrate oneself before him. khadam, collective plural of khādim, “servants”, here the palace eunuchs.

sentences.t: وَجَاءَتِ الْجَوَارِى الْحِسَانُ وَالْوَصَائِفُ بِأَيْدِيهِنَّ الشُّمُوعُ الْمَوْقُودَةُ وَالطِّيبُ وَالْبَخُورُ وَآلَاتُ الطَّرَبِ
sentences.tr: wa-jāʾati al-jawārī al-ḥisānu wa-al-waṣāʾifu bi-aydīhinna al-shumūʿu al-mawqūdatu wa-al-ṭību wa-al-bakhūru wa-ālātu al-ṭarabi
sentences.l: And came the slave-girls, the beautiful-ones, and the maids, in their(f.)-hands the candles, the lit-ones, and the perfume and the incense and the instruments of the music.
sentences.i: Then the beautiful slave-girls and the maids came in, carrying lighted candles, perfume, incense and instruments of music.
sentences.n: ḥisān, plural of ḥasana, “beautiful”. waṣāʾif, plural of waṣīfa, a young maidservant. bi-aydīhinna, “in their hands”: the bi- means “in”. ālāt al-ṭarab, “instruments of delight”, musical instruments. The print writes the final yāʾ of al-jawārī as ى.

sentences.t: فَأَمَرَ الْمَلِكُ الْمُغَنِّيَاتِ أَنْ يَجْلِسْنَ فَجَلَسْنَ فِي أَمَاكِنِهِنَّ
sentences.tr: fa-amara al-maliku al-mughanniyāti an yajlisna fa-jalasna fī amākinihinna
sentences.l: And the king commanded the singing-women that they(f.)-sit, and they(f.)-sat in their(f.)-places.
sentences.i: The king bade the singing-girls be seated, and they sat down in their places.
sentences.n: al-malik, “the king”, is the caliph: the text uses the two words freely of Hārūn. amara takes the person ordered as its object and what is ordered with an, “that”. The shadda in المغنّيات is the print's own.

sentences.t: وَجَاءَتْ شَمْسُ النَّهَارِ فَجَلَسَتْ عَلَى كُرْسِيٍّ بِجَانِبِ سَرِيرِ الْخَلِيفَةِ وَصَارَتْ تُحَدِّثُهُ
sentences.tr: wa-jāʾat Shamsu al-Nahāri fa-jalasat ʿalā kursiyyin bi-jānibi sarīri al-khalīfati wa-ṣārat tuḥaddithuhu
sentences.l: And Shams al-Nahār came and sat on a chair at the side of the couch of the caliph, and began talking-to-him.
sentences.i: Shams al-Nahār came and sat on a chair beside the caliph's throne and began to talk with him.
sentences.n: bi-jānib, “at the side of”: the bi- here means “at”. ṣāra with an imperfect, “began to”, a colloquial auxiliary common in the Nights. The shadda in تحدّثه is the print's own.

sentences.t: كُلُّ ذَلِكَ وَأَبُوالْحَسَنِ وَعَلِيُّ بْنُ بَكَّارٍ يَنْظُرَانِ وَيَسْمَعَانِ وَالْخَلِيفَةُ لَمْ يَرَهُمَا
sentences.tr: kullu dhālika wa-Abū al-Ḥasani wa-ʿAliyyu ibnu Bakkārin yanẓurāni wa-yasmaʿāni wa-al-khalīfatu lam yarahumā
sentences.l: All that, and Abū al-Ḥasan and ʿAlī son of Bakkār the-two watching and listening, and the caliph did-not see-the-two.
sentences.i: All this while Abū al-Ḥasan and ʿAlī ibn Bakkār were watching and listening, and the caliph did not see them.
sentences.n: kull dhālika wa-…, “all that, while …”: the wa- opens a clause of what was going on meanwhile. yanẓurāni wa-yasmaʿāni, “the two watch and listen”, are dual. lam yarahumā, “he did not see the two”: the jussive of raʾā, which drops its final vowel.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ الْخَلِيفَةَ صَارَ يُمَازِحُ وَيَلْعَبُ مَعَ شَمْسِ النَّهَارِ وَهُمْ فِي هَنَأٍ وَسُرُورٍ
sentences.tr: thumma inna al-khalīfata ṣāra yumāziḥu wa-yalʿabu maʿa Shamsi al-Nahāri wa-hum fī hanaʾin wa-surūrin
sentences.l: Then indeed the caliph began jesting and playing with Shams al-Nahār, and they (were) in ease and joy.
sentences.i: Then the caliph began to jest and play with Shams al-Nahār, and they were all at ease and full of joy.
sentences.n: thumma inna, “then indeed”, the storyteller's way of moving on; inna puts its subject in the accusative (al-khalīfata). The print writes هنأ for hanāʾ (هناء), “ease, well-being”, without the long ā; it is kept and pointed as the letters stand, hanaʾ. hum, “they”, masculine plural, takes in the whole company.

sentences.t: فَأَمَرَ الْمَلِكُ بِفَتْحِ الْقُبَّةِ فَفُتِحَتْ وَشَرَعُوا طِيقَانَهَا وَأَوْقَدُوا الشُّمُوعَ حَتَّى صَارَ الْمَكَانُ وَقْتَ الظَّلَامِ كَالنَّهَارِ
sentences.tr: fa-amara al-maliku bi-fatḥi al-qubbati fa-futiḥat wa-sharaʿū ṭīqānahā wa-awqadū al-shumūʿa ḥattā ṣāra al-makānu waqta al-ẓalāmi ka-al-nahāri
sentences.l: And the king commanded the opening of the dome, and it-was-opened; and they-threw-open its-windows and lit the candles, until the place became, (at) the time of the darkness, like the day.
sentences.i: The king ordered the domed pavilion to be opened. It was opened, its windows were thrown wide and the candles lit, until in the dark of night the place was as bright as day.
sentences.n: amara bi- again takes the thing ordered: bi-fatḥ al-qubba, “the opening of the dome”. sharaʿa, “open (a door or window) wide onto the outside”. ṭīqān, plural of ṭāq, an arch, and so an arched window. ka-al-nahār, “like the day”: ka- means “like”.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ الْخَدَمَ صَارُوا يَنْقُلُونَ آلَاتِ الْمَشْرُوبِ
sentences.tr: thumma inna al-khadama ṣārū yanqulūna ālāti al-mashrūbi
sentences.l: Then indeed the servants began carrying the implements of the drink.
sentences.i: Then the servants began to carry in the drinking vessels.
sentences.n: ālāt, “implements”: ālāt al-mashrūb are the cups, jugs and other gear for wine, as ālāt al-ṭarab above are the instruments of music.

sentences.t: قَالَ أَبُوالْحَسَنِ فَرَأَيْتُ آلَاتِ الْمَشْرُوبِ وَمِنَ التَّحَائِفِ لَمْ تَرَعَيْنِي مِثْلَهَا وَأَوَانِيَ مِنَ الذَّهَبِ وَالْفِضَّةِ وَسَائِرِ أَصْنَافِ الْمَعَادِنِ وَالْجَوَاهِرِ مِمَّا يَقْصُرُ عَنْهُ الْوَصْفُ حَتَّى خُيِّلَ لِي أَنِّي فِى الْمَنَامِ لِكَثْرَةِ مَا دَهِشْتُ مِمَّا رَأَيْتُ
sentences.tr: qāla Abū al-Ḥasani fa-raʾaytu ālāti al-mashrūbi wa-mina al-taḥāʾifi lam tara ʿaynī mithlahā wa-awāniya mina al-dhahabi wa-al-fiḍḍati wa-sāʾiri aṣnāfi al-maʿādini wa-al-jawāhiri mimmā yaqṣuru ʿanhu al-waṣfu ḥattā khuyyila lī annī fī al-manāmi li-kathrati mā dahishtu mimmā raʾaytu
sentences.l: Said Abū al-Ḥasan: And I-saw implements of the drink, and of the rarities (such as) my-eye did-not see the-like-of-them, and vessels of the gold and the silver and the rest of the kinds of the metals and the jewels, of-what the description falls-short of-it; until it-was-made-to-seem to-me that I (was) in the sleep, for the muchness of what I-was-amazed at-what I-saw.
sentences.i: Abū al-Ḥasan said: “I saw drinking vessels, and rarities whose like my eye had never seen, and vessels of gold and silver and of every other kind of metal and precious stone, past all describing, until I thought I must be dreaming, so amazed was I by what I saw.”
sentences.n: Here the narration passes for a moment to Abū al-Ḥasan himself, speaking in the first person, “said Abū al-Ḥasan: and I saw …”, as if the storyteller were quoting an eyewitness; the next sentence returns to the third person. التحائف is the print's form: the usual plural of tuḥfa, “a rare, precious object”, is tuḥaf (التحف), as in the previous night. It is kept and pointed taḥāʾif, as if from a singular taḥīfa. The print runs tara ʿaynī, “my eye saw”, together as one word (ترعيني); after lam, tarā takes its jussive tara. mimmā yaqṣuru ʿanhu al-waṣf, “of what description falls short of”, that is, beyond describing. khuyyila lī, “it was made to seem to me”; the shadda in خيّل is the print's own. li-kathrat mā, “because of how much”: the li- gives the cause.

sentences.t: وَأَمَّا عَلِيُّ بْنُ بَكَّارٍ فَمِنْ حِينَ فَارَقَتْهُ شَمْسُ النَّهَارِ كَانَ مَطْرُوحًا فِى الْأَرْضِ مِنْ شِدَّةِ الْوَجْدِ وَالْغَرَامِ
sentences.tr: wa-ammā ʿAliyyu ibnu Bakkārin fa-min ḥīna fāraqathu Shamsu al-Nahāri kāna maṭrūḥan fī al-arḍi min shiddati al-wajdi wa-al-gharāmi
sentences.l: And as-for ʿAlī son of Bakkār, from (the) time Shams al-Nahār parted-from-him he was cast-down on the ground from the intensity of the longing and the passion.
sentences.i: As for ʿAlī ibn Bakkār, from the moment Shams al-Nahār left him he had lain stretched on the ground, overcome by the violence of his longing and passion.
sentences.n: wa-ammā … fa-, “as for … then”, turns the story back to ʿAlī. min ḥīna, “from the time when”: ḥīn before a verb is commonly left undeclined, with fatḥa. fī al-arḍ, “in the ground”, where English says “on”. wajd and gharām, “longing” and “passionate love”, the lovesick's stock pair.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا أَفَاقَ صَارَ يَنْظُرُ إِلَى هَذِهِ الْأَشْيَاءِ الَّتِي لَا يُوجَدُ مِثْلُهَا
sentences.tr: fa-lammā afāqa ṣāra yanẓuru ilā hādhihi al-ashyāʾi allatī lā yūjadu mithluhā
sentences.l: And when he came-to, he began looking at these things which is-not found their-like.
sentences.i: When he came to himself he began to gaze at these things, whose like is nowhere to be found.
sentences.n: afāqa, “come round (from a faint)”. allatī lā yūjadu mithluhā, “which their like is not found”: the pronoun -hā in mithluhā points back to the things.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لِأَبِي الْحَسَنِ يَا أَخِي إِنِّي أَخَافُ أَنْ يَنْظُرَنَا الْخَلِيفَةُ أَوْ يَعْلَمَ حَالَنَا وَمَا أَكْثَرُ خَوْفِي إِلَّا عَلَيْكَ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla li-Abī al-Ḥasani yā akhī innī akhāfu an yanẓuranā al-khalīfatu aw yaʿlama ḥālanā wa-mā aktharu khawfī illā ʿalayka
sentences.l: And he-said to Abū al-Ḥasan: O my-brother, indeed I fear that the caliph see-us or know our-state; and the most of my-fear is not except for-you.
sentences.i: And he said to Abū al-Ḥasan, “My brother, I am afraid the caliph may see us or find out how things stand with us; and my fear is chiefly for you.
sentences.n: li-Abī al-Ḥasan, “to Abū al-Ḥasan”: the li- marks the one spoken to. naẓara with a direct object, “see” (yanẓuranā, “see us”), is colloquial; Classical says naẓara ilā. wa-mā aktharu khawfī illā ʿalayka, “and the greater part of my fear is only for you”: mā … illā, “not … except”, restricts. khāfa ʿalā, “fear for”. The shadda in الّا is the print's own.

sentences.t: وَأَمَّا أَنَا فَإِنِّي أَعْلَمُ بِنَفْسِي أَنِّي هَالِكٌ لَا مَحَالَةَ وَمَا هَلَاكِي إِلَّا بِسَبَبِ الْعِشْقِ وَالْغَرَامِ وَفَرْطِ الْوَجْدِ وَالْهُيَامِ وَفِرَاقِ الْأَحْبَابِ بَعْدَ الِاقْتِرَابِ
sentences.tr: wa-ammā anā fa-innī aʿlamu bi-nafsī annī hālikun lā maḥālata wa-mā halākī illā bi-sababi al-ʿishqi wa-al-gharāmi wa-farṭi al-wajdi wa-al-huyāmi wa-firāqi al-aḥbābi baʿda al-iqtirābi
sentences.l: And as-for me, indeed I know of myself that I (am) perishing, no escape; and my-perishing is not except by-reason-of the love and the passion, and the excess of the longing and the love-madness, and the parting of the beloved-ones after the drawing-near.
sentences.i: As for me, I know in my own heart that I am doomed past all help; and nothing is my ruin but love and passion, longing beyond measure and love's madness, and parting from the beloved after being so near.
sentences.n: ʿalima bi-, “know of”: bi-nafsī, “of myself”, in my own heart. lā maḥālata, “there is no avoiding (it)”, inevitably. bi-sabab, “by reason of”: the bi- means “by”. The nouns run in rhyming pairs, al-gharām … al-huyām, al-aḥbāb … al-iqtirāb. huyām, the frenzy of a lover who wanders out of his wits.

sentences.t: وَأَرْجُو مِنَ اللَّهِ أَنْ يُخَلِّصَنَا مِنْ هَذِهِ الْوَرْطَةِ
sentences.tr: wa-arjū mina Allāhi an yukhalliṣanā min hādhihi al-warṭati
sentences.l: And I-hope from God that He-deliver-us from this predicament.
sentences.i: I pray God to deliver us from this predicament.”
sentences.n: rajā … min, “hope (for something) from (someone)”. warṭa, a pit or quagmire, and so any scrape there is no getting out of.

sentences.t: وَلَمْ يَزَلْ عَلِيُّ بْنُ بَكَّارٍ وَأَبُوالْحَسَنِ يَنْظُرَانِ مِنَ الرَّوْشَنِ إِلَى الْخَلِيفَةِ وَمَا هُوَ فِيهِ مِنَ السُّرُورِ حَتَّى تَكَامَلَتِ الْحَضْرَةُ بَيْنَ يَدَيْهِ
sentences.tr: wa-lam yazal ʿAliyyu ibnu Bakkārin wa-Abū al-Ḥasani yanẓurāni mina al-rawshani ilā al-khalīfati wa-mā huwa fīhi mina al-surūri ḥattā takāmalati al-ḥaḍratu bayna yadayhi
sentences.l: And ʿAlī son of Bakkār and Abū al-Ḥasan ceased-not, the-two looking from the balcony at the caliph and what he (was) in-it of the joy, until the company was-complete between his-hands.
sentences.i: ʿAlī ibn Bakkār and Abū al-Ḥasan went on watching from the balcony the caliph and all the merriment he was in, until the whole company had gathered before him.
sentences.n: lam yazal stands in the singular before its two subjects, as a verb that comes first usually does; yanẓurāni, which follows them, is dual. ḥaḍra, “presence”, here the company in attendance on the caliph; takāmalat, “became complete”.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ الْخَلِيفَةَ الْتَفَتَ إِلَى جَارِيَةٍ مِنَ الْجَوَارِي وَقَالَ هَاتِي مَا عِنْدَكِ يَاغَرَامُ مِنَ السَّمَاعِ الْمُطْرِبِ فَأَخَذَتِ الْعُودَ وَأَصْلَحَتْهُ وَأَنْشَدَتْ تَقُولُ
sentences.tr: thumma inna al-khalīfata iltafata ilā jāriyatin mina al-jawārī wa-qāla hātī mā ʿindaki yā Gharāmu mina al-samāʿi al-muṭribi fa-akhadhati al-ʿūda wa-aṣlaḥathu wa-anshadat taqūlu
sentences.l: Then indeed the caliph turned to a slave-girl of the slave-girls and said: Bring what (is) with-you(f.), O Gharām, of the hearing, the delighting. And she-took the lute and set-it-right and recited, saying:
sentences.i: Then the caliph turned to one of the slave-girls and said, “Let us have what delightful music you have, Gharām.” She took up the lute, tuned it, and sang:
sentences.n: hātī, “give, bring”, the feminine of an imperative that has no other forms in use. Gharām, the singer's name, means “passionate love”. samāʿ, “hearing”, and so music listened to; muṭrib, “moving to delight (ṭarab)”. The print runs yā Gharām together as one word (ياغرام). aṣlaḥa, “put right”, of a lute “tune”.

sentences.t:
وَمَا وَجْدُ اَعْرَابِيَّةٍ بَانَ اَهْلُهَا * فَحَنَّتْ اِلى بَانَ الْحِجَازِ وَرَنْدِهِ
اِذَا اَنَسَتْ رَكْبًا تَكَفَّلَ شَوْقُهَا * بِنَارِ قِرَاهُ وَالدُّمُوْعُ بِوِرْدِهِ
بِاَعْظَمَ مِنْ وَجْدِي بِحِبِّي وَاِنَّمَا * يَرَى اَنَّنِي اَذْنَبْتُ ذَنْبًا بِوُدِّهِ
sentences.tr:
wa-mā wajdu aʿrābiyyatin bāna ahluhā * fa-ḥannat ilā bāni al-Ḥijāzi wa-randihi
idhā ānasat rakban takaffala shawquhā * bi-nāri qirāhu wa-al-dumūʿu bi-wirdihi
bi-aʿẓama min wajdī bi-ḥibbī wa-innamā * yarā annanī adhnabtu dhanban bi-wuddihi
sentences.l:
And not (is) the longing of a Bedouin-woman (whose) people departed * and she-yearned toward the ben-tree of the Ḥijāz and its rand-shrub,
(who), when she-glimpsed a riding-party, her-longing took-charge * of the fire of its guest-meal, and the tears of its watering, —
greater than my-longing for my-beloved; and yet * he-thinks that I have-sinned a sin by loving-him.
sentences.i:
No Bedouin woman whose people have moved away, and who yearns for the ben-trees and the laurel of the Ḥijāz,
whose longing, when she sights a band of riders, lights the fire to cook their welcome, and whose tears give them water,
feels a longing greater than mine for my beloved; and yet he thinks that in loving him I have done wrong.
sentences.n: The pointing is the print's own. The poem is a single comparison that runs across all three lines: wa-mā wajdu aʿrābiyyatin …, “and the longing of a Bedouin woman … is not”, opens it in line 1; line 2 goes on describing the woman; only line 3 completes it, bi-aʿẓama min wajdī, “greater than my longing”: no Bedouin woman's longing is greater than mine. The bi- before aʿẓam is the bi- that may stand on the predicate after negative mā; it adds emphasis and is not translated. Line 1: bāna ahluhā, “her people have gone away”, plays on bān, the ben-tree, a slender, sweet-scented tree of Arabia, and rand, a fragrant shrub often taken for the bay laurel: the plants of the home she longs for. The print points the second word bāna, with fatḥa, as if it were the verb again; as a noun after ilā it should be bāni, and is transliterated so. Line 2: the print's اَنَسَتْ is read ānasat, “she caught sight of” (آنَسَتْ), as the metre (ṭawīl) requires; the alif has no madda in the print. qirā is the meal given to guests, and its fire the one a host lights to cook it and to guide travellers in; wird is the watering of travellers. Her burning longing serves the riders for that fire, and her tears for their water: she welcomes them because they may bring news of her people. Line 3: ḥibb, “beloved”; wudd, “love”; bi-ḥibbī, “for my beloved”, and bi-wuddihi, “by loving him”, each with bi-.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَتْ شَمْسُ النَّهَارِ هَذَا الشِّعْرَ مَالَتْ مِنْ عَلَى كُرْسِيِّهَا الَّذِي هِيَ جَالِسَةٌ عَلَيْهِ وَسَقَطَتْ إِلَى الْأَرْضِ مَغْشِيًّا عَلَيْهَا وَغَابَتْ عَنِ الْوُجُودِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿat Shamsu al-Nahāri hādhā al-shiʿra mālat min ʿalā kursiyyihā alladhī hiya jālisatun ʿalayhi wa-saqaṭat ilā al-arḍi maghshiyyan ʿalayhā wa-ghābat ʿani al-wujūdi
sentences.l: And when Shams al-Nahār heard this verse, she-leaned from upon her-chair which she (was) sitting on-it, and fell to the ground, fainted upon-her, and was-absent from the being.
sentences.i: When Shams al-Nahār heard these verses, she slid sideways off the chair she sat on and fell to the ground in a swoon, lost to the world.
sentences.n: min ʿalā, “from upon”, that is, “off”: two prepositions stacked. maghshiyyan ʿalayhā, “fainted”, literally “covered over, upon her”: the participle stays masculine and the pronoun on ʿalā carries the person. ghābat ʿan al-wujūd, “she was absent from existence”, lost all awareness.

sentences.t: فَقَامَ الْجَوَارِي وَاحْتَمَلْنَهَا
sentences.tr: fa-qāma al-jawārī wa-iḥtamalnahā
sentences.l: And the slave-girls rose and carried-her.
sentences.i: The slave-girls rose and carried her away.
sentences.n: qāma, masculine singular, stands before a feminine plural subject; once the girls are named, the next verb, iḥtamalna, is feminine plural. A verb that comes first need not agree, but here even the gender slips, a Middle Arabic touch.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا نَظَرَ إِلَيْهَا عَلِيُّ بْنُ بَكَّارٍ مِنَ الرَّوْشَنِ وَقَعَ مَغْشِيًّا عَلَيْهِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā naẓara ilayhā ʿAliyyu ibnu Bakkārin mina al-rawshani waqaʿa maghshiyyan ʿalayhi
sentences.l: And when ʿAlī son of Bakkār looked at-her from the balcony, he-fell fainted upon-him.
sentences.i: When ʿAlī ibn Bakkār saw her from the balcony, he too fell down in a faint.
sentences.n: maghshiyyan ʿalayhi, “fainted”, as with Shams al-Nahār just before, now with the masculine pronoun on ʿalā.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ أَبُوالْحَسَنِ إِنَّ الْقَضَاءَ قَسَمَ الْغَرَامَ بَيْنَكُمَا بِالسَّوِيَّةِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla Abū al-Ḥasani inna al-qaḍāʾa qasama al-gharāma baynakumā bi-al-sawiyyati
sentences.l: And Abū al-Ḥasan said: Indeed the decree has-divided the passion between-you-two in the equal-share.
sentences.i: Abū al-Ḥasan said, “Fate has shared out love's torment between you two in equal measure.”
sentences.n: al-qaḍāʾ, what God has decreed, fate. bi-al-sawiyya, “in equal shares”: bi- of manner.

sentences.t: فَبَيْنَمَا هُمَا يَتَحَدَّثَانِ وَإِذَا بِالْجَارِيَةِ الَّتِي أَطْلَعَتْهُمَا الرَّوْشَنَ جَاءَتْهُمَا وَقَالَتْ يَا أَبَا الْحَسَنِ انْهَضْ أَنْتَ وَرَفِيقُكَ وَانْزِلَا فَقَدْ ضَاقَتْ عَلَيْنَا الدُّنْيَا
sentences.tr: fa-baynamā humā yataḥaddathāni wa-idhā bi-al-jāriyati allatī aṭlaʿathumā al-rawshana jāʾathumā wa-qālat yā Abā al-Ḥasani inhaḍ anta wa-rafīquka wa-inzilā fa-qad ḍāqat ʿalaynā al-dunyā
sentences.l: And while the-two (were) talking-together, behold, the slave-girl who had-made-them-go-up the balcony came-to-them and said: O Abū al-Ḥasan, rise, you and your-companion, and go-down(you-two), for the world has-grown-narrow upon-us.
sentences.i: While the two of them were talking, the slave-girl who had taken them up to the balcony came to them and said, “Abū al-Ḥasan, get up, you and your friend, and go down, for we are in desperate straits.
sentences.n: wa-idhā bi-, “and behold”, as before. aṭlaʿathumā al-rawshana, “she made the two go up to the balcony”, form IV with two objects. inhaḍ is addressed to Abū al-Ḥasan alone, then inzilā to both. ḍāqat ʿalaynā al-dunyā, “the world has grown narrow on us”: no way out is left. The shadda in يتحدّثان is the print's own.

sentences.t: وَأَنَا خَائِفَةٌ أَنْ يَظْهَرَ الْأَمْرُ أَوْ يَعْلَمَ بِكُمَا الْخَلِيفَةُ فَإِنْ لَمْ تَنْزِلَا فِي هَذِهِ السَّاعَةِ مُتْنَا
sentences.tr: wa-anā khāʾifatun an yaẓhara al-amru aw yaʿlama bikumā al-khalīfatu fa-in lam tanzilā fī hādhihi al-sāʿati mutnā
sentences.l: And I (am) afraid that the matter appear or the caliph know of-you-two; so if you-two-do-not go-down in this hour, we-have-died.
sentences.i: I am afraid the affair will come to light, or the caliph will learn that you are here; and if you do not go down this very moment, we are dead.”
sentences.n: ʿalima bi-, “know of, find out about”: the verb takes its object with bi-. mutnā, “we have died”, a perfect for what is sure to follow.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ أَبُوالْحَسَنِ وَكَيْفَ يَنْهَضُ هَذَا الْغُلَامُ مَعِي وَلَاقُدْرَةَ لَهُ عَلَى النُّهُوضِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla Abū al-Ḥasani wa-kayfa yanhaḍu hādhā al-ghulāmu maʿī wa-lā qudrata lahu ʿalā al-nuhūḍi
sentences.l: And Abū al-Ḥasan said: And how will this youth rise with-me, and no power (is) to-him over the rising?
sentences.i: Abū al-Ḥasan said, “And how is this young man to get up and come with me, when he has no strength to rise?”
sentences.n: The print runs ولا قدرة together. lā qudrata lahu, “there is no power to him”: lā denying the whole class, its noun in -a, and li- of possession. qudra ʿalā, “power to do”.

sentences.t: فَصَارَتِ الْجَارِيَةُ تَرُشُّ عَلَيْهِ مَاءَ الْوَرْدِ حَتَّى أَفَاقَ مِنْ غَشْيَتِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-ṣārati al-jāriyatu tarushshu ʿalayhi māʾa al-wardi ḥattā afāqa min ghashyatihi
sentences.l: And the slave-girl began sprinkling on-him water of the rose until he-came-to from his-swoon.
sentences.i: So the slave-girl set about sprinkling rose-water on him until he came round from his faint.
sentences.n: ṣāra with an imperfect, “began to …, set about …”.

sentences.t: فَحَمَلَهُ أَبُو الْحَسَنِ وَأَسْنَدَتْهُ الْجَارِيَةُ وَنَزَلَابِهِ مِنَ الرَّوْشَنِ وَمَشَيَا قَلِيلًا
sentences.tr: fa-ḥamalahu Abū al-Ḥasani wa-asnadathu al-jāriyatu wa-nazalā bihi mina al-rawshani wa-mashayā qalīlan
sentences.l: And Abū al-Ḥasan carried-him and the slave-girl propped-him, and the-two went-down with-him from the balcony and the-two walked a-little.
sentences.i: Abū al-Ḥasan took him up and the slave-girl held him steady, and between them they brought him down from the balcony and went on a little way.
sentences.n: The print runs نزلا به together. nazalā and mashayā are dual, “the two”: Abū al-Ḥasan and the girl, carrying ʿAlī between them. nazala bi-, “go down with”, that is, bring down: bi- of accompaniment.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ فَتَحَتِ الْجَارِيَةُ بَابًا صَغِيرًا مِنَ الْحَدِيدِ وَأَخْرَجَتْ أَبَا الْحَسَنِ وَعَلِيَّ بْنَ بَكَّارٍ
sentences.tr: thumma fataḥati al-jāriyatu bāban ṣaghīran mina al-ḥadīdi wa-akhrajat Abā al-Ḥasani wa-ʿAliyya ibna Bakkārin
sentences.l: Then the slave-girl opened a small door of the iron and brought-out Abū al-Ḥasan and ʿAlī son of Bakkār.
sentences.i: Then the slave-girl opened a small iron door and let Abū al-Ḥasan and ʿAlī ibn Bakkār out.
sentences.n: min al-ḥadīd, “of iron”: min of the material. ʿAliyya, accusative as the second object of akhrajat, takes no nunation before ibn, as a name followed by its father's name does not.

sentences.t: فَرَأَيَا مَصْطَبَةً عَلَى شَاطِئِ الدِّجْلَةِ فَجَلَسَا عَلَيْهَا
sentences.tr: fa-raʾayā maṣṭabatan ʿalā shāṭiʾi al-Dijlati fa-jalasā ʿalayhā
sentences.l: And the-two saw a bench on the bank of the Tigris, and the-two sat on-it.
sentences.i: They saw a stone bench on the bank of the Tigris and sat down on it.
sentences.n: maṣṭaba, a raised bench of stone or brick built against a wall or by the water. The Tigris, Dijla, normally takes no article; the print gives it one, al-Dijla.

sentences.t: فَصَفَّقَتِ الْجَارِيَةُ بِيَدَيْهَا فَأَتَاهَا رَجُلٌ فِي زَوْرَقٍ صَغِيرٍ فَقَالَتْ لَهُ خُذْ هَذَيْنِ الشَّابَّيْنِ وَأَطْلِعْهُمَا عَلَى الْبَرِّ الثَّانِي
sentences.tr: fa-ṣaffaqati al-jāriyatu bi-yadayhā fa-atāhā rajulun fī zawraqin ṣaghīrin fa-qālat lahu khudh hādhayni al-shābbayni wa-aṭliʿhumā ʿalā al-barri al-thānī
sentences.l: And the slave-girl clapped with her-two-hands, and there-came-to-her a man in a small skiff; and she said to-him: Take these two youths and bring-them-up onto the land the second.
sentences.i: The slave-girl clapped her hands, and a man came to her in a little skiff. She said to him, “Take these two young men and set them ashore on the far bank.”
sentences.n: bi-yadayhā, “with her two hands”: bi- of the instrument. zawraq, a small boat, a skiff. aṭliʿhumā ʿalā al-barr al-thānī, “bring them up onto the second land”, that is, land them on the other bank; barr is dry land as against water.

sentences.t: فَنَزَلَا فِى الزَّوْرَقِ فَلَمَّا قَذَفَ بِهِمَا الرَّجُلُ وَفَارَقَا الْبُسْتَانَ نَظَرَ عَلِيُّ بْنُ بَكَّارٍ إِلَى قَصْرِ الْخِلَافَةِ وَالْقُبَّةِ وَالْبُسْتَانِ وَوَدَّعَهُمْ بِهَذَيْنِ الْبَيْتَيْنِ
sentences.tr: fa-nazalā fī al-zawraqi fa-lammā qadhafa bihimā al-rajulu wa-fāraqā al-bustāna naẓara ʿAliyyu ibnu Bakkārin ilā qaṣri al-khilāfati wa-al-qubbati wa-al-bustāni wa-waddaʿahum bi-hādhayni al-baytayni
sentences.l: And the-two went-down into the skiff; and when the man pushed-off with-the-two and they-two parted-from the garden, ʿAlī son of Bakkār looked at the palace of the caliphate and the dome and the garden, and bade-them-farewell with these two verses:
sentences.i: They went down into the skiff, and when the boatman had pushed off with them and they had left the garden behind, ʿAlī ibn Bakkār looked back at the caliph's palace, the dome and the garden, and bade them farewell in these two lines:
sentences.n: qadhafa bihimā, “he cast off with them”: qadhafa, “throw, cast”, is used of working the oars (miqdhāf, “oar”), and bi- is of accompaniment. The print writes fī with ى. waddaʿahum, “he bade them farewell”: the masculine plural pronoun takes in palace, dome and garden together. bi-hādhayni al-baytayni, “with these two verses”: bi- of the means. The shadda in ودّعهم is the print's own.

sentences.t:
مَدَدْتُ اِلَى التَّوْدِيعِ كَفًّا ضَعِيفَةً * وَاُخْرَى عَلَى الرَّمْضَاءِ تَحْتَ فُؤَادِي
فَلَا كَانَ هٰذَا آخِرُ الْعَهْدِ بَيْنَنَا * وَلَا كَانَ هٰذَا الزَّادُ آخِرُ زَادِي
sentences.tr:
madadtu ilā al-tawdīʿi kaffan ḍaʿīfatan * wa-ukhrā ʿalā al-ramḍāʾi taḥta fuʾādī
fa-lā kāna hādhā ākhiru al-ʿahdi baynanā * wa-lā kāna hādhā al-zādu ākhiru zādī
sentences.l:
I-stretched-out to the farewell a hand weak * and another upon the scorching-ground beneath my-heart.
So may this not be the last of the meeting between-us, * and may this provision not be the last of my-provision.
sentences.i:
I held out one feeble hand to bid farewell, and pressed the other to the burning beneath my heart.
May this not be the last that we see of each other, nor this provision the last that I carry away.
sentences.n: The pointing is the print's own. Metre ṭawīl. kaff, “hand”, is feminine, hence ḍaʿīfatan and ukhrā. al-ramḍāʾ is ground baked hot by the sun; here it is the fire of love in his breast, on which he lays his other hand. fa-lā kāna, lā with a perfect, is a wish: “may it not be”. ʿahd here is meeting, time spent together, as in ākhir al-ʿahd, “the last one sees of someone”. Twice the print points ākhiru in the nominative where kāna's predicate would normally be ākhira; it can stand if hādhā is taken as the predicate set first and ākhiru … as the subject, “may the last … not be this”, and it is kept as printed. zād, provisions for a journey: this last sight is what he carries with him.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ الْجَارِيَةَ قَالَتْ لِلْمَلَّاحِ أَسْرِعْ بِهِمَا فَصَارَ يَقْذِفُ لِأَجْلِ السُّرْعَةِ وَالْجَارِيَةُ مَعَهُمْ
sentences.tr: thumma inna al-jāriyata qālat li-al-mallāḥi asriʿ bihimā fa-ṣāra yaqdhifu li-ajli al-surʿati wa-al-jāriyatu maʿahum
sentences.l: Then indeed the slave-girl said to the boatman: Hurry with-the-two; so he-began rowing for-the-sake-of the speed, and the slave-girl with-them.
sentences.i: Then the slave-girl said to the boatman, “Make haste with them,” and he set to rowing as fast as he could, the slave-girl with them in the boat.
sentences.n: thumma inna, “then indeed”, a storyteller's link that moves the tale on. asriʿ bihimā, “hurry with them”: bi- of accompaniment. li-ajli, “for the sake of”: li- of purpose. maʿahum, masculine plural “with them”: the boatman and the two young men. The shadda in الملّاح is the print's own.

sentences.t: وَأَدْرَكَ شَهْرَزَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُبَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka Shahrazāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿani al-kalāmi al-mubāḥi
sentences.l: And morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent from the permitted speech.
sentences.i: And morning overtook Shahrazād, and she ceased the speech allowed her.
